title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Dead

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
This is a book about dust and money, about death and reinvention, about a city that devours its own.
And it begins, magnificently, with a body in the Thames.
To help us unpack it, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of Dickens.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads with a craftsperson's eye — always asking how the thing is made, why this word, why this image, why here.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he brings the world behind the novel, the institutions, the poverty, the law, the things Dickens's first readers would have recognised with a cold shudder.

And Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is about character, not programme — that what endures in Dickens is the moral imagination, not the polemics.
A warm welcome to all three of you.
Let's begin with the atmosphere Dickens builds from the very first pages — because this novel announces itself like no other.
What strikes me immediately is that Dickens doesn't ease you in — he plunges you into sensory assault.
The fog passage is a masterclass in what I'd call graduated suffocation.
He takes you from grey at the margins to brown to browner to, finally, rusty-black at the heart of the city.
It's a chromatic descent — colour as moral geography.
But the line that stops me every time is this one — let me read it:

"Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither."
That opposition — animate and inanimate — is the novel's whole engine, set up in a single sentence.
The city is simultaneously alive and dead, and so, we will discover, is almost every character in it.
Eleanor is quite right about the architecture of that sentence — but I want to resist the temptation to make the fog merely symbolic.
Dickens was a man who walked London obsessively, who knew its smells and its textures with the intimacy of a native creature.
When he writes of gaslights with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing themselves to be night-creatures, he is giving us something felt, not merely theorised.
The atmosphere is the precondition for everything that follows — the fog of moral confusion through which individual characters must find their own way.
And Dr. Johnson would have said, I think, that the power lies precisely in that — the particular made universal through the pressure of imagination.
I take Edmund's point — but the fog isn't innocent geography, either.
Victorian London's fogs were partly natural and very substantially industrial — coal smoke, effluent, the literal byproduct of the economy Dickens is elsewhere so ferocious about.
And this novel is ferocious about the economy of waste — nowhere more pointedly than in the dustheap passages.
Dickens turns to address the governing classes directly — and I think it's one of the most controlled acts of rage in the English novel.
He writes — and the syntax itself is the trap:
"you must off with your honourable coats for the removal of it, and fall to the work with the power of all the queen's horses and all the queen's men, or it will come rushing down and bury us alive."
The irony in that phrase — honourable coats — is surgical.
These men of honour have built the mountain of pretentious failure, and now Dickens tells them, bluntly, that it will kill everyone if they don't shift it themselves.
And James's phrase — the syntax is the trap — that's exactly right.
Dickens builds the sentence as a conditional — you must do this, or this will happen — and the doom is grammatically inevitable.
He's not pleading — he's pronouncing.
One may admire the rhetoric and still wonder whether haranguing lords and gentlemen in a serial novel quite persuades anyone.
Burke's view — and I think it was Dickens's deeper instinct too — was that reform flows from sympathy, not indictment.
And it is the characters of this novel — Boffin, Bella, Eugene — who carry that work, not the polemical passages.
Edmund's scepticism is entirely courteous and entirely wrong.
The Harmon Murder case shows us exactly how public attention circulates — and dissipates.
Dickens captures this with one of his most astonishing extended metaphors.

"like the tides on which it had been borne to the knowledge of men, the Harmon Murder — as it came to be popularly called — went up and down, and ebbed and flowed, now in the town, now in the country, now among palaces, now among hovels, now among lords and ladies and gentlefolks, now among labourers and hammerers and ballast-heavers, until at last, after a long interval of slack water it got out to sea and drifted away."
He names every rung of the social ladder — palaces to hovels, lords to ballast-heavers — and then watches the whole thing dissolve into indifference.
That is not sympathy producing reform — that is satire diagnosing failure.
And the professional world Dickens sketches around this — Mortimer Lightwood's law office — is its own small masterpiece of gothic comedy.
Mortimer describes his situation with magnificent world-weariness.

"Whether, in that shabby rook's nest, he is always plotting wisdom, or plotting murder; whether he will grow up, after so much solitary brooding, to enlighten his fellow-creatures, or to poison them; is the only speck of interest that presents itself to my professional view."
A lawyer whose single clerk is his only professional interest — and that interest is whether the boy will turn sage or murderer.
The law in this novel is an institution so hollowed out that its representatives find Gothic speculation more compelling than actual work.
The shabby rook's nest overlooking a burial ground — it's a remarkable emblem for where this novel situates the law.
Dust heaps, murder, fog, a body in the river — and already, just pages in, a society that seems to be eating itself alive.
In our next segment, we turn to the characters at the centre of it all — and ask what Dickens does with the idea of inheritance.

segments.title: The Architecture of Deception: How Dickens Built Harmon's Secret

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, piece by piece, and ask how it works and why it matters.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the most elaborately engineered deceptions in Victorian fiction: the triple identity of John Harmon, John Rokesmith, and Julius Handford.
To help us unpick the architecture of that deception, I'm joined by three exceptional readers.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads for the craft — for the way a sentence is built, an image planted, an identity concealed.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will ground us in what disguise and social death actually meant in the world Dickens was depicting.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who insists, against all fashionable pressure, on reading novels as moral adventures of individual character.
Eleanor, Dickens actually breaks the fourth wall in this novel to discuss the Harmon mystery — let's start there.
Yes, and it's a remarkably bold move — Dickens steps outside the story entirely to address his readers directly, in what functions almost as a postscript to the novel.
He's responding to a specific critical complaint — that he had laboured to conceal Rokesmith's true identity when, in fact, he'd been doing the opposite.
The passage is worth hearing in full, because the confidence of it is quite extraordinary.

He writes: 'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
The symmetry of that construction is perfect — 'at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest' — it's almost a chiasm, and it's designed to make the critics look foolish.

And then he extends that artistic confidence into something rather lovely — the notion that an artist 'may perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will concede him a little patience.'
It's Dickens at his most assured — not defensive, but serene.
Serene is the right word, and I'd add something further: that statement is also a rebuke — delivered with perfect courtesy, but a rebuke nonetheless.
There is a distinction, which Dickens understood very well, between suspense and mystification.
Suspense is moral — it asks us to care about what will happen to a person.
Mystification is merely technical — it withholds information for the pleasure of the reveal.
What Dickens claims here, and what I think he largely achieves, is that the Harmon deception belongs to the first category, not the second.
The question was never merely 'who is Rokesmith?' — the question was always what kind of man he would prove to be.
There's a dimension here that neither of you has yet touched on, and it's perhaps the most legally peculiar aspect of the whole scheme.
When Harmon decides to remain 'dead,' he isn't simply playing a social game — he is, in a quite real sense, erasing his own legal personhood.
And the scheme, as he explains it, began with something almost innocently opportunistic.

He tells us: 'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
Common sailors' dresses — that detail matters enormously in class terms.
A man of property disguising himself as a working seaman is not merely adopting a costume — he is passing across a social boundary that Victorian England treated as nearly absolute.
And yet the plot spirals almost immediately out of Harmon's control.
Eleanor, when we look at the moment of the reveal — the removal of the disguise — there's something almost theatrically precise in how Dickens renders it.
Theatrically precise is exactly right, and what makes the scene technically extraordinary is that Dickens refuses to give us a single stable identity emerging from the disguise.
When the oakum-headed sailor removes the false hair, he becomes — simultaneously, impossibly — two people at once.
Listen to how the prose performs that multiplication.
'He became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world.'
And then — in the very next sentence — 'For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world.'
The repetition is precise, almost incantatory — Dickens uses identical syntax to say that two identities are each, separately, the same as a third.
It's logically dizzying, and it's entirely deliberate — identity here is not resolved but multiplied.
The syntax is remarkable, but I want to press on the moral content of that multiplication, because I think we risk losing it in admiration of the technique.
Dickens takes considerable care to show us that the deception did not begin from vanity or malice.
The relevant passage in chapter thirty-one is one of the most searching psychological passages in the novel.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.'
The rhythm of that sentence — the long subordinate clause of cause before the main clause of consequence — enacts the very accumulation it describes.
Character shaped by a childhood of harm drifts, almost without volition, into harm of its own devising.
That is not a social argument — that is a moral one, and it is the deeper architecture of the whole Harmon plot.
I don't dispute the moral reading — but I'd suggest the social and moral arguments are not separable here, and Dickens is quite explicit about why.
The 'distrust engendered by his wretched childhood' is not an abstract psychological condition — it is specifically the distrust produced by wealth and its corrupting reach.
The phrase 'the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence' is doing serious institutional work.
Harmon senior's money has functioned like a malign legal instrument — touching everyone around it and converting them.
And John's dilemma when he finally sees the Boffins is presented in almost legal terms — as a choice between two forms of wrong from which there is no procedurally correct exit.
That sense of being trapped — of a deception that grows beyond the deceiver's control — connects beautifully to the ghost imagery that runs through Harmon's self-reflection.
Edmund, that churchyard passage — where Harmon speaks of himself as one of the dead — seems to me one of the most haunting moments in the novel.
It is, and the word I would reach for is loneliness rather than horror — though the two are not far apart in this passage.
Dickens finds a formulation of extraordinary precision for the condition of the socially dead man.

'It is a sensation not experienced by many mortals — to be looking into a churchyard on a wild windy night, and to feel that I no more hold a place among the living than these dead do, and even to know that I lie buried somewhere else, as they lie buried here.'
'A spirit that was once a man could hardly feel stranger or lonelier, going unrecognized among mankind, than I feel.'
What is remarkable is the double burial — he knows where the corpse mistaken for him lies, and that knowledge doubles his isolation rather than relieving it.
This is not Gothic atmosphere for its own sake — it is the precise phenomenology of a man who has voluntarily abdicated his own existence.
And Dickens extends that ghost metaphor into the chapter that follows with extraordinary structural discipline.
Chapter thirty-one opens with an image that manages to be both darkly comic and genuinely moving.
'The sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon all night long was not conducive to sound sleep.'
The 'sexton-task' is metaphorical — Rokesmith has spent the night mentally burying his own former self — but Dickens renders it with the weight and rhythm of literal labour.

And then the resolution: 'No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place.'
That phrase 'the state of existence out of which it had departed' — he's describing life itself as a place you can depart from and then observe from the outside.
It's a genuinely vertiginous idea, and Dickens delivers it with complete formal control.
There's one more piece of the mechanism I think we should examine before moving on, because it's easy to overlook in all the philosophical grandeur.
The physical exchange that makes the whole plot possible — the exchange of clothes with Radfoot — is rendered with an almost documentary precision that I find fascinating.
Harmon recalls it like a man reconstructing evidence, pausing to verify his own account.
And then — the detail that lodges in the memory — the black man in the linen jacket who brings the coffee and 'never looked at me.'
That witness who is trained not to witness — it captures something very specific about how the invisible labour of such scenes was structured.
And then Harmon's compulsive self-interrogation: 'I am so far literal and exact? Literal and exact, I am certain.' — the repetition telling us he is a man who dare not trust his own memory.

The man who constructs identities cannot entirely trust the identity that is doing the constructing — which is rather a brilliant structural irony to plant at the heart of the novel's great deception.
We'll be returning to the consequences of that deception — and to the woman at the centre of it — when we come back.

segments.title: Bella's Education: Gold, Goodness, and the Self

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three extraordinary readers of this novel, and we're turning our attention to what I think is one of Dickens's most quietly daring achievements: the education of Bella Wilfer.
Bella arrives in this novel as a self-declared mercenary, a young woman who has decided, with some style and no small measure of honesty, that she intends to marry for money.
And yet by the novel's end she has become something richer and stranger than that simple description allows.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is with us — novelist, teacher of creative writing, and the person I most want beside me when a sentence refuses to give up its secrets.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — he knows what wealth actually meant in Victorian England, and he will not let us sentimentalise it.
And Sir Edmund Leigh joins us as our conscience and our corrective — a reader who insists that what happens in a novel happens first to a soul, not a social class.
Let's begin with that famous mirror scene — Bella alone in her room, interrogating her own reflection.
Eleanor, you've written about the way novelists use moments of self-confrontation. What is Dickens doing here?
The looking-glass is doing extraordinary structural work in this scene.
Dickens has set up this habit of Bella's — addressing herself in mirrors — and here he springs it on us at full rhetorical force.
Because what she says to herself is genuinely remarkable in its self-exposure.
She arrives at this internal catechism:

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
She knows the thought is right. She knows it is her own thought. And she hates it for being spoken aloud by someone else.
That triple structure — assent, recognition, revulsion — is Dickens mapping a very precise moral psychology.
And then the final turn of the screw: she names herself 'you inconsistent little Beast' — comic, yes, but genuinely diagnostic.
What strikes me historically is the precision of Bella's predicament as Dickens has constructed it.
She is, in the novel's own language, a 'mercenary young person' — and that is not merely a moral failing, it is a completely rational response to the marriage market of the 1860s.
Women of Bella's position had virtually no economic independence outside of marriage.
So what she is being educated out of is not simply greed — it is a survival strategy that the society has imposed on her.
And Dickens is careful — characteristically careful — about this.
Her father, the Cherub, articulates the stakes with that wonderful mock-legal syntax:

'the certain mercenary young person distantly related to myself... felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive.'
That anaphoric list — right and wrong, true and false, just and unjust — that is the full moral inventory of a human being.
Dickens is saying: wealth is not a test of virtue. It is a test of whether you still know what virtue is.
I find myself in rare agreement with James on the structural stakes, though I should like to come at the thing from a rather different angle.
What Dickens gives us in Bella's education is not primarily a social argument but a drama of moral perception.
Consider the moment when Bella looks at Boffin and sees, with terrible clarity, what prosperity has made of him.
Dickens renders it in a single stroke:
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
'The once open face' — that is devastating. Three words that carry an entire history of lost innocence.
And what Bella does with this perception is the mark of moral seriousness: she does not simply pity Boffin, she reads herself in him.
That capacity for self-implication in the corruption of another — that is what separates genuine moral growth from mere good fortune.
Edmund's point about self-implication opens something I think is crucial to how Dickens constructs Bella as a character.
Because for much of the novel, Bella is constitutionally incapable of that depth of attention.
The narrator describes her nature with this extraordinary compound phrase:
'wayward, playful, affectionate nature, giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose, and capricious because it was always fluttering among little things.'
'Giddy for want of the weight' — that inversion is everything. The problem is not too much weight but too little.
She is not corrupt; she is unballasted. And what the novel's plot provides, through Boffin's performed corruption, is precisely the ballast she needs.
The structure of her education is not punishment but provision — she is given the weight her soul was always reaching for.
I want to come back to something Edmund introduced — this idea of Bella reading herself in Boffin's corruption — because there is a pedagogical design here that is almost ruthlessly deliberate.
When the truth finally comes out, Bella herself articulates the lesson in words that could have come from a dissenting preacher.
She speaks Boffin's unspoken reasoning back to him:

'This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in; but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking.'
That phrase — 'a glaring instance' — is the language of demonstration, of empirical proof.
Boffin's strategy is not moral lecture but living experiment: show, do not tell.

And what I find historically interesting is that this is precisely the logic of certain reformist traditions — the belief that the poor could not be argued out of ignorance but could be shown out of it.
James will forgive me if I resist the reformist framing, though I think he has identified something real.
What moves me most in Bella's arc is not the lesson administered but the moment she claims it as her own — when she asks to be tested.
To Rokesmith she says, with a gravity that the comic Bella of earlier chapters could not have summoned:
'Try me through some reverse, John — try me through some trial — and tell them after that, what you think of me.'
That repetition — 'try me through some reverse, try me through some trial' — is the cadence of someone who has genuinely reckoned with herself.
She is not asking to be believed. She is asking to be proved.
That is a distinction which novelists of lesser moral seriousness rarely bother to make.
And that is what makes the mirror scene at the beginning so retroactively poignant.
Early Bella interrogates herself in the glass with comic exasperation: 'you inconsistent little Beast.'
Late Bella asks to be tested by reality, not by reflection.
She has moved from the looking-glass to the world.
That is Dickens's structural argument in miniature.
From the looking-glass to the world — I think that is a fine place to pause before we turn to the novel's other great education: the river, and what it takes, and what it returns.
Thank you, Eleanor, James, Edmund — that was beautifully argued, all three.

segments.title: Money and Moral Corruption: The Boffins and Victorian Greed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the series devoted to close reading and rigorous discussion of Charles Dickens's final completed novel.
Today we're examining one of the novel's most unsettling obsessions: what money does to a person's soul.
We'll be looking at the Boffins, at the monstrous dust contractor who haunts the novel's backstory, and at the assorted predators who circle new wealth like hungry birds.
With me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a clock — always looking for the mechanism behind the beauty.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — what these institutions actually were, what poverty truly cost, and why Dickens's anger about all of it still lands.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, reads the novel as a moral drama — about character, conscience, and the kind of goodness that either survives wealth or doesn't.
Let's begin where the novel begins its indictment of greed — with the man who made the Dust Mounds, John Harmon's father.
What strikes me first about the Dust Contractor passages is that Dickens doesn't let himself be merely angry.
He deploys Mortimer as his narrator, and that choice is surgical — the drawling, ironic social voice keeps the horror at one remove, which makes it worse, not better.
Listen to how Mortimer frames the father's cruelty as a kind of moral achievement.
'The moral being — I believe that's the right expression — of this exemplary person, derived its highest gratification from anathematizing his nearest relations and turning them out of doors.'
'Exemplary' — and Mortimer uses that word bone-dry — is the engine of the whole sentence.
It says: society has provided no adequate language of condemnation for this man, so I will borrow the language of praise and invert it.
That structural irony is doing what the law and the church and polite society refuse to do — it's calling the thing evil.
And the daughter's story sharpens the legal edge of all that irony considerably.
Under Victorian law, a father had essentially absolute authority over an unmarried daughter's choice of husband — and over her property until marriage transferred that authority to a husband.

So when Mortimer says the father 'chose a husband for her, entirely to his own satisfaction and not in the least to hers,' that isn't merely cruelty — it is the legal norm exercised without restraint.
And what the daughter says in protest is extraordinary.
'Such a marriage would make Dust of her heart and Dust of her life — in short, would set her up, on a very extensive scale, in her father's business.'
That phrase — 'her father's business' — is Dickens connecting the commercial and the personal with absolute precision.
The Dust trade is not merely a metaphor — it's the literal accumulation of what society throws away — and the father treats human beings by the same logic.
He is the business.
One mustn't lose sight of what Dickens is also doing morally here — not merely sociologically.
The father's sin is not that he is wealthy, but that he has made wealth the exclusive measure of human worth — which is a corruption of the soul, not merely the wallet.
And Dickens marks the enormity of it with that single devastating image.
'Immediately, the venerable parent — on a cold winter's night, it is said — anathematized and turned her out.'
'On a cold winter's night, it is said' — that parenthetical is everything.
Mortimer introduces the faintest note of oral tradition — 'it is said' — as though the detail is too terrible to own outright, yet too important to omit.
The cold night individualizes the cruelty. It gives it weather.
'It gives it weather' — that's exactly right, and I want to carry that thought forward to the Boffin passages, because Dickens does something even more formally audacious there.
He gives the corruption a clock.
Boffin at breakfast is recognisably himself — warm, unguarded.
But then Dickens writes something that operates almost like a stage direction for a soul.
'It was as the day went on that the clouds gathered, and the brightness of the morning became obscured.'
And then — as if that weren't enough — 'One might have said that the shadows of avarice and distrust lengthened as his own shadow lengthened, and that the night closed around him gradually.'
The shadow of avarice literally mimics the movement of the sun across the day.
It's a metaphor that becomes cosmological — which is exactly the scale Dickens wants us to feel.
The daily rhythm Dickens describes is, I think, historically very precise — and it connects to something Boffin himself articulates with startling candour.
Boffin's new wealth doesn't simply change his tastes or his address — it changes what he understands his obligations to be.
He explains it to Mrs Boffin with a directness Dickens rarely allows a character making this kind of argument.
'Our old selves wouldn't do here, old lady. Haven't you found that out yet? Our old selves would be fit for nothing here but to be robbed and imposed upon.'
There is, note, no claim that the new self is better — only that it is armoured.

This is the Victorian discourse of respectability turned inside out — the logic that says wealth demands a certain hardness, not because hardness is virtuous, but because softness will be preyed upon.
And Dickens is showing us that this logic is not eccentric — it was widely held.
Though one must say: Dickens also makes Boffin articulate the class dimension of that hardness with almost parodic explicitness.
The passage about the Secretary is, to my mind, the most uncomfortably funny thing in this section of the novel.
Boffin is pacing the room — Dickens gives him 'a trot,' which is beautifully undignified — and he announces his new philosophy of employment.
'A man of property owes a duty to other men of property, and must look sharp after his inferiors.'
He has absorbed the ideology of his new class with the enthusiasm of a convert.
What Dickens understands — and what I think is the novel's genuine moral insight — is that ideologies of class are not imposed from above.
They are eagerly taken up by those who have newly arrived and wish to belong.
And the scene where Boffin's corruption reaches its visible peak — that black morning with Rokesmith — is written with a kind of gothic intensity that I find astonishing.
Dickens gives us the darkest line almost parenthetically.

'The look he directed at the Secretary's retiring figure was so cunningly malignant, that Bella would have sat astounded and indignant, even though he had not gone the length of secretly threatening Rokesmith with his clenched fist as he closed the door.'
'Secretly' — that word is doing something precise.
The gesture is invisible to Rokesmith — it's for no audience.
Which means the malice has gone entirely inward — it no longer needs a witness to exist.
Against all of that darkness, I want to insist on the passage Dickens writes about what the Boffins were — before wealth complicated everything.
Because Dickens is not making an argument that wealth inevitably destroys — he's making a more precise and more difficult argument about moral foundation.
He writes of the Boffins that they 'had guided themselves so far on in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do right.'
And then he stakes out something that reads almost like a theorem.
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
That is not a sentimental statement.
It is almost juridical — a principle about the differing propagation of vice and virtue across time.
The Boffins' goodness, even under the pressure of wealth, has consequences that outlast the corruption.
That theorem, as you call it, is the moral axis of everything Dickens constructs around the Dust Mounds.
What Wegg represents — that extraordinary figure with his pocket-handkerchief and his performed gravity — is the logical terminus of self-deception in the service of greed.
Dickens is quite specific about what kind of impostor Wegg is.
'He ranged with that very numerous class of impostors, who are quite as determined to keep up appearances to themselves, as to their neighbours.'
'To themselves' — that is the key.
Wegg is not a cynical schemer who privately acknowledges his fraud.
He has deceived himself first — and that is what makes him, and all those who resemble him, genuinely dangerous.

What emerges from all of this is a picture of money as something that doesn't simply corrupt — it reveals, it accelerates, and sometimes, as Dickens insists, it fails to extinguish what was genuinely good.
In our next segment, we'll follow the Harmon plot more closely — what the inheritance demand reveals about love, identity, and whether a man can choose to refuse his own name.

segments.title: Reading Bella's Wit: Dickens's Comic Voice and the Wayward Heart

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — in every sense of that word.
I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the novel's most delightful and complicated achievements: the character of Bella Wilfer.
Bella is funny, vain, self-aware, and genuinely good — sometimes all in the same paragraph — and Dickens uses her comic voice to do some of his deepest moral work.
With me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for how effects are constructed sentence by sentence is simply unmatched.
Professor James Blackstone brings the weight of legal and social history — he keeps us honest about what Dickens's world actually looked and felt like.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, who reads novels as moral fables — and whose patience with fashionable interpretations is, shall we say, finite.
Let's begin with Bella alone in her room, talking to herself in the looking-glass — a scene that is, I think, one of the funniest and most searching in the whole novel.
What strikes me first about that scene is the architecture of Bella's self-interrogation.
Dickens gives her the looking-glass as a prop — a literal device — but it becomes a kind of confessional mirror.
She doesn't ask a narrator to judge her; she turns the judgment on herself with that devastating final phrase.
Listen to the rhythm of it — Dickens builds the logic in short declarative steps, then releases it all in one:

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That word 'Beast' — with a capital B in the text — lands like a verdict.
Dickens has essentially let Bella prosecute and convict herself, and the comedy is inseparable from the moral clarity.
Eleanor is quite right about the moral clarity — but I'd go further.
What Dickens is doing here is something rather classical: he is showing us a conscience that works.
Bella knows perfectly well that her reaction is wrong. She knows it instantaneously.
The comedy is not satirical in any cutting social sense — it is the comedy of a good nature catching itself in the act of being bad.
Dr. Johnson observed that the test of a person's character is what they do when no one is watching.
Bella is being watched — by herself — and she does not flinch from what she sees.
That is, I think, Dickens at his very best.
I admire both readings, and I don't wish to flatten the comedy with context — but the context is actually rather important here.
Bella's dependency on Mr Boffin is total. She is, in the novel's own terms, a girl who was left as a legacy to a stranger.
When she calls herself an 'inconsistent little Beast' for disparaging her benefactor, she is describing a psychological trap that was very real for dependent women of that era.
You cannot afford to think ill of the person who holds your future — so you turn the criticism inward instead.
The self-laceration is funny, yes — but it also tells us something about who is permitted to be dissatisfied and at what cost.
James, I think that's right — and Dickens pushes even harder at it in a later chapter, where Bella escalates the self-accusation.
There's a glorious moment where she runs out of polite terms and lands on the most wonderfully compressed piece of self-criticism in the whole book.
'Such a shallow, cold, worldly, Limited little brute!'
Dickens tells us she brings out that last adjective — 'Limited' — with, quote, 'culminating force.'
The escalation from 'shallow' to 'cold' to 'worldly' to 'Limited' is almost musical — each word a slightly sharper key.
And 'Limited' with a capital L is extraordinary — it sounds almost like a company name, a commercial designation, which is entirely the point.
The capital L is a masterstroke — I grant Dickens that without reservation.
But I want to hold onto what James was saying about inwardness, because I think it connects to a passage I find more moving than any of these comic turns.
There is a scene at the Lock — Riderhood's apparent death and revival — that Dickens constructs as a kind of mirror image of Bella's moral world.
Where Bella's bad self is exposed through comedy, Riderhood's bad self is exposed through something far bleaker — the withdrawal of human warmth.
Dickens writes it with a kind of terrible symmetry:
'As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him.'
The prose itself is a chiasmus — warmth and coldness, life and rejection, swapped perfectly across a single sentence.
Bella earns back the warmth of those around her because she does the work of moral self-scrutiny. Riderhood never does.
Edmund has put his finger on something that I find genuinely troubling about the novel's moral economy, however.
The crowd's compassion for Riderhood is entirely conditional on his being unconscious — on his character being, as it were, suspended.
Dickens calls his face 'low, bad, unimpressible' — and the crowd reads those features back from memory the moment he begins to revive.
Now, Dickens clearly intends this as satire on the crowd's conditional mercy — he is not endorsing it.
But the novel also never grants Riderhood the possibility of what it grants Bella — the interior life, the self-interrogating wit, the path to redemption.
And that, I think, is a class distinction dressed as a moral one.
I expected that reading, James, and I respect it — but I think it mistakes the novel's project.
Riderhood is not denied an interior life because he is poor. He is denied one because he has chosen, repeatedly and deliberately, to be what he is.
Dickens is a moralist, not a determinist. Character is not merely circumstance.
What I find so remarkable is how Dickens resolves the Bella question — not through another looking-glass scene, but through motherhood.
There's a passage late in the novel where Bella has her baby, and Dickens uses the child as a kind of refracting mirror for Bella's vanity — but now the vanity is entirely innocent.
He writes of her finding her own dimples reflected in the baby's face, 'as if she were looking in the glass without personal vanity.'
The looking-glass motif returns — but it is purged of its self-accusation.
And then Dickens does something structurally daring — he challenges the entire world to match what he's about to describe:
'The world might have been challenged to produce another baby who had such a store of pleasant nonsense said and sung to it, as Bella said and sung to this baby.'
'Pleasant nonsense' — that phrase is doing everything. It is the 'inconsistent little Beast' turned outward, made generous, made joyful.
And then there is the moment when Bella sees Mr Boffin again — the man she had dismissed, whose influence she had resisted — and finds him utterly transformed.
The prose here is almost dizzy with Bella's bewilderment, because she cannot reconcile what she sees with what she remembers.
Dickens asks the question for her:
'What had become of all those crooked lines of suspicion, avarice, and distrust, that twisted his visage then?'
'Crooked lines' — the language of physiognomy, but also of moral mapping. The face as a record of the soul's choices.
And now those lines are simply gone — because the performance of avarice is over, and the real Mr Boffin can return.
That's the comedy completing its moral arc — and it does so with a lightness of touch that I find genuinely moving.
What a journey — from Bella prosecuting herself in the mirror to finding her own dimples in her daughter's face to the crooked lines vanishing from Mr Boffin's.
Dickens is tracking something about self-knowledge — about what it costs, and what it earns you.
Thank you to Eleanor, James, and Edmund for a conversation that has been, I think, as pleasantly nonsensical and as morally serious as Bella herself.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment — stay with us.

segments.title: The Weight of Circumstance: Character Under Pressure in Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — and examine what makes it one of the great achievements of Victorian fiction.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sits at the very heart of this novel: what does pressure do to a person?
Not the pressure of plot, but the deeper kind — social pressure, moral pressure, the pressure of wanting to be someone other than who you were born to be.
To explore that, I'm joined by three extraordinary minds.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great gift is showing us how literary technique is never merely technique — it's the novelist's moral intelligence in action.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the real workhouses, the real schoolrooms, the real cost of poverty in Victorian England.

And Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, brings a beautifully sceptical intelligence — he reads novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance, and he keeps the rest of us honest.
Let's begin with Bradley Headstone — perhaps the most agonising portrait in all of Our Mutual Friend.
What strikes me first about the Headstone portrait is the extraordinary audacity of that opening catalogue — the word 'decent' hammered seven times in a single sentence.
It's a rhetorical trap, actually.
We nod along — yes, decent, decent, decent — and by the time we've accepted his decency, Dickens has slipped a knife between the ribs: 'as if there were a want of adaptation between him and it.'
The costume fits, but the man inside doesn't.
And then comes that astonishing warehouse metaphor — let me read it, because it really must be heard whole.

'The arrangement of his wholesale warehouse, so that it might be always ready to meet the demands of retail dealers — history here, geography there, astronomy to the right, political economy to the left — natural history, the physical sciences, figures, music, the lower mathematics, and what not, all in their several places.'
It's devastating, and it's funny, and it's desperately sad — all three at once.
Knowledge as inventory, never as illumination.
Eleanor is exactly right that the passage is funny — but I'd want to press on why it's so specifically painful, because the institutional context matters enormously here.
Headstone is the product of the new elementary school system — the monitorial schools, the pupil-teacher schemes — a system built entirely on mechanical rote learning.
A working-class child of genuine intelligence could rise through it, but the price was exactly what Dickens describes: you became the system that formed you.
The word 'mechanically' — it appears four times in short succession — isn't a metaphor Dickens is imposing from the outside.
It's the actual pedagogy.

And the consequence Dickens identifies — 'a suspicious manner, or a manner that would be better described as one of lying in wait' — is the psychological cost of a life spent being tested and found wanting.
What we're watching is a man deformed by the only ladder available to him.
I don't dispute any of that historical texture, and James makes it vivid.
But I think we are in danger of making Headstone merely a victim of his system, when Dickens is doing something more searching than that.

The narrator tells us quite precisely that it was 'the face belonging to a naturally slow or inattentive intellect that had toiled hard to get what it had won, and that had to hold it now that it was gotten.'
The trouble is constitutional, in part.
He is not a brilliant man made rigid by bad schooling — he is a man of limited natural gifts who has clawed his way up and lives in perpetual terror of exposure.
That is a different, and in some ways more interesting, moral predicament — and one that transcends any particular educational dispensation.
Edmund, I think you're right about the constitutional element, and it makes the later chapters all the more terrible.
Because in chapter forty-four we see what happens when all that rigidity finally cracks — and Dickens frames it philosophically, not just dramatically.
He says something that I find genuinely radical about the psychology of great criminals — the narrator pauses the whole narrative to deliver it.
'If great criminals told the truth — which, being great criminals, they do not — they would very rarely tell of their struggles against the crime.'
'Their struggles are towards it.'
Four words.
The entire mythology of the tempted innocent fighting his baser nature — demolished in four words.
That passage is extraordinary, and also deeply uncomfortable — because it refuses sympathy without refusing complexity.

Headstone is 'tied up all day with his disciplined show upon him, subdued to the performance of his routine of educational tricks' — and then at night he 'broke loose at night like an ill-tamed wild animal.'
The schoolmaster's entire public existence is performance — and what lies beneath the performance is rage.

This is Dickens identifying something that criminologists would only begin to articulate a generation later: that extreme social constraint, enforced daily over years, can produce violence not in spite of discipline but through it.
The Victorian school system created Headstone — and then had no idea what to do with him.
I want to sit with that image of the 'bloody shore' a moment, because I think Eleanor was right to isolate it — it is one of Dickens's finest single sentences.
He writes: 'They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not to recede from it.'
What arrests me is the word 'gain.'
One gains a shore — as one gains a prize, a victory.
The crime is not a fall — it is an achievement, in the terrible grammar of Headstone's psychology.
And what makes this a great moral novel — not merely a social document — is that Dickens refuses to let the system entirely off the hook either.
Both things are true simultaneously, which is exactly how tragedy works.
And against all that violence and self-enclosure, Dickens sets Lizzie Hexam — who is also under enormous pressure, and who transforms rather than collapses.
Eleanor, there's a passage where Lizzie speaks about what Eugene's presence means to her, and I think it's one of the most quietly extraordinary speeches in the whole novel.
It really is, and what makes it remarkable technically is that Lizzie gives this speech in a moment of apparent passivity — she is explaining to another character why she doesn't want to move away.
And yet inside that apparent passivity is one of the most complex accounts of how moral aspiration actually works — how we use love as an ethical compass.
She says — and this needs to be heard carefully:

'I should lose a kind of picture of him — or of what he might have been, if I had been a lady, and he had loved me — which is always with me, and which I somehow feel that I could not do a mean or a wrong thing before.'
An imaginary portrait of an impossible man — a man he never was and never could be — is her moral guardian.
That is a profoundly subtle piece of moral psychology.
That passage moves me greatly — and I think it illuminates the contrast with Headstone more sharply than any critical commentary could.
Headstone's love for Lizzie destroys him — it becomes obsession, rage, murder.
Lizzie's love — which is also unrequited in its most fundamental form, for the Eugene she imagines could never exist in their world — refines her.
And she finds an extraordinary image for it at the very end of the speech — the change in her hands, coarse from rowing, now made supple by her new work.
'Which were coarse, and cracked, and hard, and brown when I rowed on the river with father, and are softened and made supple by this new work as you see them now.'
The body itself becomes the record of moral transformation.
Dickens is at his very best here — concrete, physical, utterly free of sentimentality.
The hands matter enormously to me as a historian, because they are doing real class work in this passage.
Lizzie's coarse, rowed hands mark her as working class — as labour.
The 'new work' that softens them is the needlework she takes up — still labour, still manual, but of the kind associated with modest femininity.
Dickens isn't pretending that class has been transcended — only that within its limits, something authentic and ennobling has occurred.
And that seems to me far more honest than a fairy-tale rescue.
Which brings us to the final, devastating chapter in Headstone's arc — after the crime, when the weight of what he's done becomes something almost geological.
Edmund, you've been waiting to talk about this passage, I think.
It is perhaps the passage in the entire novel where Dickens's moral imagination is most fully extended — and it is almost unbearable to read.
He describes the three-fold weight Headstone carries: 'the knowledge of what he had done, of that haunting reproach that he might have done it so much better, and of the dread of discovery.'
That second element stops the breath — 'the haunting reproach that he might have done it so much better.'
He is tormented not by guilt in any recognisable moral sense — but by wounded professional pride.
Even in his crime, he cannot escape the examiner's mentality — the sense that he has fallen below his own standard.
And then comes that image — let me read it exactly as Dickens writes it, because the comparison is almost shockingly stark.

'The overweighted beast of burden, or the overweighted slave, can for certain instants shift the physical load, and find some slight respite even in enforcing additional pain upon such a set of muscles or such a limb.'
'Not even that poor mockery of relief could the wretched man obtain, under the steady pressure of the infernal atmosphere into which he had entered.'
The word 'infernal' is precise — not metaphorical, or rather, metaphorical in the most exact sense: he has made his own hell, and entered it voluntarily.
The slave comparison will not have landed lightly for Victorian readers in 1865, the year Our Mutual Friend was completed.
The American Civil War had only just ended — debates about slavery and labour were everywhere in English public discourse.
And Dickens places the overworked animal and the slave on the same line — they have the same standing in his comparison.
The point is not that Headstone is like a slave — the point is that even a slave has a physical recourse that he does not.
He has entered a condition of suffering that has no name in the social vocabulary of Victorian England — and no escape.
What haunts me is the phrase 'steady pressure of the infernal atmosphere' — it's not an event, it's a condition.
Dickens doesn't describe Headstone suffering moments of guilt — he describes him inhabiting guilt as a climate.
And it's precisely because there is nowhere to shift the weight — no muscle he can ease, no limb he can favour — that the prose rhythm itself seems to go airless.
Compare that to the opening passage, where every sentence has energy — satirical, furious, inventive.
By the end, the prose is as trapped as the man inside it.
Three lives under pressure — Headstone deformed by ambition and finally destroyed by it, Lizzie refined by a love she turns into a moral vision, and Eugene standing at the centre of both.
What this novel keeps insisting, I think, is that circumstance does not determine character — but it does supply the pressure that reveals it.
My profound thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Sir Edmund Leigh — this has been a genuinely illuminating hour.
We'll be back in our next episode to follow the money — literally — as we examine the novel's obsession with dust, inheritance, and the strange alchemy of wealth in Our Mutual Friend.
We've been following the dust heaps, the river, the money, the disguises — all the threads Dickens weaves through this extraordinary novel.
And now, in our closing segment, we want to ask the largest question of all: what survives?
What does Dickens believe can endure — in a world built on waste, on pretence, on the suffering of the poor?
Eleanor, James, Edmund — I want to draw on everything we've discussed today, and on Dickens's own words from the novel's closing chapters.
What strikes me, coming to the end of Our Mutual Friend, is how carefully Dickens has arranged his survivals.
The people who make it through — who are genuinely transformed — are not the ones who fought the system on its own terms.
They're the ones who were broken open by love, or by loss, and rebuilt from something truer.
Bella Wilfer is the great example, and there's a passage where she tries to articulate it — and almost can't.
She says — and she's covering her face with her hands as she says it —

"It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife."
That phrase — 'so unworthy a wife' — is not self-flagellation for its own sake.
It's the voice of someone who has genuinely measured herself and found the measurement humbling.
Eleanor is quite right, and I think this is the moral centre of the novel — not its politics, its individual moral drama.
Bella's transformation is, in the old sense of the word, a reformation — a forming again of the self from better materials.
And notice that it requires other people — the Boffins, John Harmon — acting with extraordinary, uncalculating generosity.
That is what Dickens believes survives: not institutions, not legislation — the capacity for individual human goodness.
Edmund, I won't quarrel with any of that — the novel's emotional truth is exactly as you describe it.
But I think you have to place that tenderness in the context of Dickens's fury — and the fury is inseparable from it.
The Postscript to the novel is among the most direct statements he ever made about the Poor Law, and it's devastating.
He writes, with controlled contempt —
"I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised."
And then he goes further: 'the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity — and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.'
That is a man who has reported from the evidence and reached a verdict.
I shan't pretend the indictment is not just — it plainly is.
But I'd observe that Dickens is attacking the administration of the law, not the principle of moral order itself.
His anger is the anger of someone who believes things should be done properly — which is, at bottom, a conservative impulse.
I'll grant you that — with the caveat that 'conservative' in Dickens's mouth would have been fighting words.
But the warning in the novel is stark, and I don't think it's merely rhetorical.
He addresses the ruling class directly — 'my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards' — and the passage is a prophecy as much as a polemic.

"When we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance."
'Impossible of continuance.' He means it as a structural prediction, not a pious hope.
And what I find so remarkable is that those two registers — the intimate and the prophetic — coexist in the same novel without fracturing it.
Bella weeping with gratitude in one chapter; the narrator thundering at Parliament in another.
That's the architecture of the whole — and Dickens knew exactly what he was doing.
In the Postscript, he talks about the design — about keeping the Harmon secret working beneath the surface across nineteen months of serial publication.

"To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design."
'Always working itself out' — that's how the whole novel operates, not just the Harmon plot.
Every thread — the dust, the river, the money, the pretence — is working itself out toward something.
That phrase is extraordinarily beautiful — 'always working itself out.'
It suggests that the meaning of a story is not declared but discovered — earned through the unfolding.
And I think that is the deepest answer to your question of what survives — the story itself.
The dust heaps are gone; the Veneerings have vanished into social oblivion; even the river keeps moving.
But the novel remains — and it keeps, as Dickens says, working itself out in the mind of whoever reads it.
I couldn't ask for a finer place to end.
Our Mutual Friend — a novel about dust, and rivers, and money, and disguise, and the extraordinary, stubborn capacity of human beings to love each other well or badly.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Edmund Leigh — three readers who have made this novel feel alive in ways I won't quickly forget.
And to you listening — thank you for spending this time with us and with Dickens.
Until next time.

It was a foggy day in London, and the fog was heavy and dark. Animate
      London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing,
      and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose
      between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.
      Gaslights flared in the shops with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing
      themselves to be night-creatures that had no business abroad under the
      sun; while the sun itself when it was for a few moments dimly indicated
      through circling eddies of fog, showed as if it had gone out and were
      collapsing flat and cold. Even in the surrounding country it was a foggy
      day, but there the fog was grey, whereas in London it was, at about the
      boundary line, dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then
      browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City—which call
      Saint Mary Axe—it was rusty-black. From any point of the high ridge
      of land northward, it might have been discerned that the loftiest
      buildings made an occasional struggle to get their heads above the foggy
      sea, and especially that the great dome of Saint Paul’s seemed to die
      hard; but this was not perceivable in the streets at their feet, where the
      whole metropolis was a heap of vapour charged with muffled sound of
      wheels, and enfolding a gigantic catarrh.

‘I am one by myself, one,’ said Mortimer, ‘high up an awful staircase
      commanding a burial-ground, and I have a whole clerk to myself, and he has
      nothing to do but look at the burial-ground, and what he will turn out
      when arrived at maturity, I cannot conceive. Whether, in that shabby
      rook’s nest, he is always plotting wisdom, or plotting murder; whether he
      will grow up, after so much solitary brooding, to enlighten his
      fellow-creatures, or to poison them; is the only speck of interest that
      presents itself to my professional view. Will you give me a light? Thank
      you.’

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.

      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

Left alone at his stall as the other ambled off, Mr Wegg subsided into his
      screen, produced a small pocket-handkerchief of a penitentially-scrubbing
      character, and took himself by the nose with a thoughtful aspect. Also,
      while he still grasped that feature, he directed several thoughtful looks
      down the street, after the retiring figure of Mr Boffin. But, profound
      gravity sat enthroned on Wegg’s countenance. For, while he considered
      within himself that this was an old fellow of rare simplicity, that this
      was an opportunity to be improved, and that here might be money to be got
      beyond present calculation, still he compromised himself by no admission
      that his new engagement was at all out of his way, or involved the least
      element of the ridiculous. Mr Wegg would even have picked a handsome
      quarrel with any one who should have challenged his deep acquaintance with
      those aforesaid eight volumes of Decline and Fall. His gravity was
      unusual, portentous, and immeasurable, not because he admitted any doubt
      of himself but because he perceived it necessary to forestall any doubt of
      himself in others. And herein he ranged with that very numerous class of
      impostors, who are quite as determined to keep up appearances to
      themselves, as to their neighbours.

Bradley Headstone, in his decent black coat and waistcoat, and decent
      white shirt, and decent formal black tie, and decent pantaloons of pepper
      and salt, with his decent silver watch in his pocket and its decent
      hair-guard round his neck, looked a thoroughly decent young man of
      six-and-twenty. He was never seen in any other dress, and yet there was a
      certain stiffness in his manner of wearing this, as if there were a want
      of adaptation between him and it, recalling some mechanics in their
      holiday clothes. He had acquired mechanically a great store of teacher’s
      knowledge. He could do mental arithmetic mechanically, sing at sight
      mechanically, blow various wind instruments mechanically, even play the
      great church organ mechanically. From his early childhood up, his mind had
      been a place of mechanical stowage. The arrangement of his wholesale
      warehouse, so that it might be always ready to meet the demands of retail
      dealers—history here, geography there, astronomy to the right, political
      economy to the left—natural history, the physical sciences, figures,
      music, the lower mathematics, and what not, all in their several places—this
      care had imparted to his countenance a look of care; while the habit of
      questioning and being questioned had given him a suspicious manner, or a
      manner that would be better described as one of lying in wait. There was a
      kind of settled trouble in the face. It was the face belonging to a
      naturally slow or inattentive intellect that had toiled hard to get what
      it had won, and that had to hold it now that it was gotten. He always
      seemed to be uneasy lest anything should be missing from his mental
      warehouse, and taking stock to assure himself.

c44:p1.text:
The state of the man was murderous, and he knew it. More; he irritated it,
      with a kind of perverse pleasure akin to that which a sick man sometimes
      has in irritating a wound upon his body. Tied up all day with his
      disciplined show upon him, subdued to the performance of his routine of
      educational tricks, encircled by a gabbling crowd, he broke loose at night
      like an ill-tamed wild animal. Under his daily restraint, it was his
      compensation, not his trouble, to give a glance towards his state at
      night, and to the freedom of its being indulged. If great criminals told
      the truth—which, being great criminals, they do not—they would
      very rarely tell of their struggles against the crime. Their struggles are
      towards it. They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not
      to recede from it. This man perfectly comprehended that he hated his rival
      with his strongest and worst forces, and that if he tracked him to Lizzie
      Hexam, his so doing would never serve himself with her, or serve her. All
      his pains were taken, to the end that he might incense himself with the
      sight of the detested figure in her company and favour, in her place of
      concealment. And he knew as well what act of his would follow if he did,
      as he knew that his mother had borne him. Granted, that he may not have
      held it necessary to make express mention to himself of the one familiar
      truth any more than of the other.

Yes, verily, my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, adapting your
      Catechism to the occasion, and by God’s help so you must. For when we have
      got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to
      relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their
      heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is
      a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance. It may not be
      so written in the Gospel according to Podsnappery; you may not ‘find these
      words’ for the text of a sermon, in the Returns of the Board of Trade; but
      they have been the truth since the foundations of the universe were laid,
      and they will be the truth until the foundations of the universe are
      shaken by the Builder. This boastful handiwork of ours, which fails in its
      terrors for the professional pauper, the sturdy breaker of windows and the
      rampant tearer of clothes, strikes with a cruel and a wicked stab at the
      stricken sufferer, and is a horror to the deserving and unfortunate. We
      must mend it, lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, or in its own
      evil hour it will mar every one of us.

      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.

c67:p58.text:
To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
c67:p58.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.
